name: Jason Rau Ankle Lock System
description: Study Jason Rau ankle-lock decisions through grips, leg position and changing opponent posture, with a focused course guide and linked control and back-take topics.
summary: The Jason Rau Ankle Lock System is a BJJGraph study framework for connecting ankle-lock control with the positional decisions created by a defender's changing posture.
overview:
Dynamic Ankle Locks provides a specific course companion for studying grips and leg position alongside seated, kneeling and standing reactions. Its syllabus extends beyond straight ankle locks to other submissions and back-take options. That distinction matters when choosing a section for a particular training session.

The plan below is BJJGraph's original study sequence. It begins with recognising whether the ankle and leg remain connected to the attacker as the defender changes posture. A lost connection can make a positional transition more sensible than continuing the original submission. Select permitted techniques with a coach, and keep advanced Aoki-lock or heel-hook branches separate from a straight-ankle-only practice objective.
key_principles: Assess the leg connection as well as the hand grip.
Name whether the defender is seated, kneeling or standing before choosing a response.
Treat a posture change as a new control problem rather than a reason to squeeze harder.
Distinguish straight ankle locks from other submissions in the course.
Keep back-take options available when the original leg connection is no longer useful.
Define allowed attacks before an entanglement round begins.

key_components.description: Compare the selected ankle grip with the leg arrangement supporting it rather than evaluating either in isolation.
key_components.purpose: Identify whether the whole position supports the attempted attack.

key_components.description: Observe the different balance and connection problems presented by a seated, kneeling or standing defender.
key_components.purpose: Choose the relevant lesson for the actual exchange.

key_components.description: Notice when the attacker can no longer maintain useful leg contact despite retaining the foot with the hands.
key_components.purpose: Avoid chasing the original finish after its positional basis is gone.

key_components.description: Compare guard recovery or a coached back-take route with a permitted secondary submission.
key_components.purpose: Make the next objective explicit instead of switching locks blindly.

implementation_sequence.description: Begin in a familiar leg entanglement and identify the grip and leg contact used in the selected lesson.
Let the partner make one small seated adjustment. Stop when either the grip or supporting leg connection ceases to control the exchange.
Use the corresponding course section to review what changes when the partner comes to their knees. Keep the entry task free of finishing pressure.
Rehearse a deliberate release or positional fallback when the legs can no longer support the original attack.
Select a coach-approved back-take or other permitted branch. Compare its required control with the option of recovering guard.

common_obstacles.obstacle: The hands retain the foot while the legs lose contact.
common_obstacles.solution: Stop and diagnose the leg-position problem instead of increasing finishing effort.

common_obstacles.obstacle: The same answer is used against every defender posture.
common_obstacles.solution: Separate seated and kneeling rounds and identify the different control requirements.

common_obstacles.obstacle: A straight-ankle drill drifts into another leg lock.
common_obstacles.solution: Name permitted attacks in advance and reset before an unagreed branch.

common_obstacles.obstacle: A back take is assumed whenever the ankle lock fails.
common_obstacles.solution: Check that the new route has its own connection and choose guard recovery when it does not.

assessment_metrics.description: Observe whether the grip and leg position work together.
Classify the defender's posture before selecting a response.
Check that the drill remains within its agreed submission scope.
Review the next objective after losing ankle-lock control.

training_methodology.drilling_approach: BJJGraph suggests two entry-and-control rounds from the same ankle-lock position: one with the partner seated and one with a slow kneeling reaction. Keep finishing pressure out of the comparison. Record whether the first loss is the hand grip or supporting leg contact, then use that observation to select a course lesson and a coached fallback.

progression_path.focus: Recognise the relationship between the ankle grip and supporting leg position.
Compare seated and kneeling defensive reactions.
Practise deliberate release and guard recovery.
Add one permitted secondary route with clear control requirements.

common_mistakes: Holding the foot after the rest of the entanglement has disappeared.
Treating all ankle-related submissions as interchangeable.
Forcing a back take without establishing its entry connection.

flashcards.question: Why examine leg position as well as the ankle grip?
flashcards.answer: The hands may retain the foot after the supporting leg contact has disappeared, leaving the original attack without useful positional control.

flashcards.question: What defender postures should be distinguished in this study plan?
flashcards.answer: Separate seated, kneeling and standing situations because each changes the connection and balance problems the attacker must solve.

flashcards.question: Does Dynamic Ankle Locks contain only straight ankle locks?
flashcards.answer: No. The listed material also includes other leg submissions and back-take options, so choose the permitted study track deliberately.

flashcards.question: What should happen when a straight-ankle drill reaches an unagreed branch?
flashcards.answer: Reset before applying the different submission and return to the techniques and endpoints agreed for that session.

flashcards.question: When is a back take a useful alternative to the ankle lock?
flashcards.answer: It is useful when its own entry connection is present; a failed ankle attack alone does not establish a viable back-take route.

flashcards.question: What should be recorded during the posture-comparison drill?
flashcards.answer: Record the defender's posture and whether the hand grip or supporting leg connection was the first part of control to fail.
